title: Apply personal hygiene principles in poultry processing

lessons.title: Why personal hygiene matters
lessons.html:
You can make food unsafe

Raw chicken meat can carry germs such as Salmonella and Campylobacter. People can also carry germs on their hands, hair, skin, nose and clothes. If you are not clean, you can put germs onto the meat. Then people who eat the chicken can get very sick. Food poisoning can be dangerous for babies, old people and sick people.

A poultry plant that sells unsafe chicken can lose its customers and can be closed. Your clean habits protect the people who eat the food, your company and your job.

Where germs come from

  • Dirty hands, especially after using the toilet, smoking or eating.
  • Hair and beards falling onto the product.
  • Coughing and sneezing.
  • Cuts and sores that are infected.
  • Dirty clothes and boots from outside.
  • Jewellery, which holds dirt and can fall into the product.

Clean areas and dirty areas

A poultry plant is divided into areas. The dirty area is where live birds are received, killed and plucked. The clean area is where carcasses are eviscerated, chilled, cut and packed. Workers from the dirty area must not walk into the clean area without changing and washing. Many plants use different coloured clothing so that supervisors can see who belongs where. Always follow the colour rules and the walkways in your plant.

Example: Lerato works in packing. At lunch she goes outside. When she comes back, she must go through the change room, put on clean protective clothing, wash her hands and step through the boot wash before she goes back to the packing line.

lessons.title: Getting ready for work
lessons.html:
Before you enter the plant

Good hygiene starts at home. Bath or shower every day. Keep your fingernails short and clean. Do not wear nail polish or false nails.

In the change room

  1. Take off your own outside clothes and put them in your locker.
  2. Take off all jewellery: rings, earrings, watches, bracelets and necklaces. A plain wedding band may be allowed in some plants; follow your plant's rule.
  3. Put on a clean hair net. All hair must be inside the net. Men with beards must also wear a beard net.
  4. Put on clean protective clothing: overall or coat, apron and gumboots.
  5. Do not take food, sweets, chewing gum, cell phones or cigarettes into the production area.

Washing your hands the right way

  1. Wet your hands with clean warm water.
  2. Put on soap.
  3. Rub all parts: palms, backs, between the fingers, thumbs, fingertips and nails, for about 20 seconds.
  4. Rinse well under running water.
  5. Dry with a paper towel or hand dryer. Do not dry on your apron.
  6. Use the hand sanitiser if the plant has it.

When to wash your hands

  • Before you start work and after every break.
  • After using the toilet.
  • After touching your face, hair or nose.
  • After touching the floor, rubbish or anything dirty.
  • After handling waste or condemned birds.

Step through the boot wash every time you enter the production area. It cleans the soles of your boots so you do not bring dirt in.

Remember: the change room, hand wash basin and boot wash are there for a reason. Skipping one step, even when you are late or the line is waiting, can undo all the other good work. If soap, paper towels or sanitiser run out, tell your supervisor straight away.

lessons.title: Good habits on the line and when you are sick
lessons.html:
Habits during work

  • Do not eat, drink, smoke or chew gum in the production area.
  • Do not spit.
  • Do not cough or sneeze over the product. Turn away and cover your mouth with your elbow, then wash your hands.
  • Do not touch your face, hair or nose while working.
  • If meat falls on the floor, do not put it back on the line. Follow the plant rule, usually putting it in the condemned or rework container.
  • Keep your knife and steel clean and put them in the steriliser (hot water) between uses as instructed.
  • Do not wear your protective clothing to the toilet, canteen or outside. Take off your apron and coat first.

Cuts and wounds

If you cut yourself, stop work and go to the first aider. Small cuts must be covered with a blue waterproof plaster. Blue is used because it is easy to see if it falls into the product. Some plants also use plasters with a metal strip so the metal detector can find them. Wear a glove over the plaster.

When you are sick

You must tell your supervisor before starting work if you have:

  • Diarrhoea or vomiting.
  • A fever, bad cough or flu.
  • Infected sores, boils or wounds on your hands or arms.
  • Discharge from your eyes, ears or nose.

The supervisor may give you other work away from the product or send you to the clinic. Do not hide illness. It is not about punishing you. It is about keeping germs away from the food.

Key points

  • Remove jewellery and wear a hair net and clean protective clothing.
  • Wash your hands properly before work, after breaks and after the toilet.
  • Never eat, smoke, spit or chew gum in the production area.
  • Cover cuts with a blue waterproof plaster and a glove.
  • Tell your supervisor if you have diarrhoea, vomiting or infected sores.
